summary: Proposes a framework for extending HTTP in a coordinated way, since many applications had proposed their own extensions that did not work together. Its status is historic.

eli5.summary: Everyone was adding different extra buttons to the web. This tried to give one tidy way to add them. It is now historic.

questions: what is the http extension framework
how do you add mandatory extensions to http
what is the m- prefix for
how do proxies handle http extensions
what does the 510 not extended error mean
subtitle: A standard way to add protocol extensions to HTTP.

tldr.problem: Many applications wanted to extend HTTP with their own features, but there was no coordinated framework, so extensions didn't work together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a framework where each extension gets a globally unique identifier (URI), and extension declarations in HTTP header fields identify which extensions apply to a message. Extensions can be mandatory (the recipient must understand them) or optional.
tldr.outcome: This is now historic, as the web moved toward other extension mechanisms like HTTP headers and content negotiation. However, the framework influenced later approaches to HTTP extensibility.

facts.label: Extension identifier format
facts.value: Absolute URI or standard HTTP header field name

today: RFC 2774 is Historic. It was published as Experimental because the Internet community was uncertain whether it represented consensus on HTTP extension design, and alternative approaches eventually became more prevalent.

sections.title: The Problem of Uncoordinated Extensions
sections.content:
HTTP was being extended in many different ways by many different applications: distributed authoring (WebDAV), collaboration tools, printing, and remote procedure calls all proposed their own extensions. These extensions were not coordinated with each other, leading to conflicts and incompatibilities.

The framework described in RFC 2774 aims to provide a common mechanism so extensions can coexist peacefully and applications can declare which extensions they require or support.
sections.eli5: Imagine a town where everyone keeps inventing new traffic rules, and nobody tells each other about them. This is how HTTP extensions were. The RFC tries to create a town announcer who tells everyone: 'Today, we're using rule X and rule Y.'

sections.title: Extension Declarations and Identifiers
sections.content:
Each extension is identified by either an absolute URI (such as http://www.company.com/extension) or by the name of a standard HTTP header field (such as Range). Every extension declaration includes the extension identifier and may include optional parameters in a consistent format.

Extension declarations appear in HTTP header fields: Man and Opt for end-to-end extensions (from client to server directly), and C-Man and C-Opt for hop-by-hop extensions (between adjacent nodes in the request chain).
sections.eli5: Think of an extension declaration as a label on a package: 'This package uses special handling rule #5.' The label tells anyone handling it what special care to take.

sections.title: Mandatory and Optional Extensions
sections.content:
Mandatory extension declarations indicate that the recipient must understand and apply the extension, or reject the request with a 510 (Not Extended) error. Optional extension declarations indicate that the recipient may apply the extension if it knows about it, or safely ignore it if it does not.

Mandatory HTTP requests must prefix their method with M- (such as M-GET). The server responds with Ext or C-Ext header fields to confirm it understood and handled the mandatory extensions.
sections.eli5: 'Mandatory' means the server must follow the special rule or give up. 'Optional' means the server can follow it if it knows how, but it's okay to ignore it. The M- prefix is like a red flag saying 'I have special rules here.'

sections.title: Processing Mandatory Requests
sections.content:
When a server receives a mandatory request (one with the M- prefix), it must: identify all mandatory extensions declared in the request, check if it supports them, and if not, return a 510 error. If it does support them, it must process the request according to the extension semantics, then respond with Ext and/or C-Ext headers to acknowledge it fulfilled the mandatory declarations.

Proxies must forward mandatory extension declarations without removing them, even if the proxy does not understand the extensions itself.
sections.eli5: It's like a restaurant: when an order says 'must be gluten-free' (mandatory), the chef either makes it gluten-free or says 'sorry, we can't.' If the chef makes it gluten-free, they write 'gluten-free' on the receipt so the customer knows.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC notes that extensions may involve dynamic installation of software, which opens the door to 'Trojan horse' attacks if untrusted extensions are executed. A malicious third party could forge an extension under a provider's name, or a provider could send malicious code disguised as an extension.

The framework itself does not solve these security problems; it simply defines a standard way to declare extensions. Implementers must make their own decisions about which extensions to trust.
sections.eli5: If you let programs automatically install themselves to handle special HTTP rules, a bad guy could sneak in bad software. The framework just says 'here's how to announce rules'; it's up to you to decide which rules are safe.

sections.title: Historical Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 2774 was published as Experimental in February 2000, reflecting mixed community views on whether it truly represented consensus on how HTTP should evolve. The document has since been made Historic.

While this specific framework did not become the standard approach to HTTP extensibility, the RFC influenced thinking about extension mechanisms and remains instructive for understanding the design challenges of protocol extensibility.
sections.eli5: This RFC tried to solve a problem, but the Internet community wasn't sure if this was the right way. Now it's marked as 'historic,' meaning people don't use it anymore, but it still teaches useful lessons.
